title: Doctoral thesis and book 'The Other Side' on Nazism and Zionism (1982–1984)
description: His 1982 Soviet dissertation on the relationship between the Nazis and the leaders of the Zionist movement in 1933–1945, published in 1984 as 'The Other Side: The Secret Relationship Between Nazism and Zionism', has been described by Jewish groups as a work of Holocaust denial (Britannica). According to passages quoted by Wikipedia (citing the Wyman Institute and other sources), the book called the figure of six million Jewish victims a 'myth' inflated by the Zionist movement for political gain and cited estimates of 'a few hundred thousand' or at most 890,000, and, according to critics, blamed Zionist agitation for the Holocaust. About ten years later Abbas said he had written it while the Palestinians were at war with Israel and that 'today I would not have made such remarks'; in a 2006 interview with Haaretz he said he had only quoted a debate among historians, called the Holocaust 'a terrible, unforgivable crime against the Jewish nation' and said 'nobody can claim I denied it'. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and others continue to cite the thesis, for example in 2018 ('a Holocaust-denier remains a Holocaust-denier').
key_facts: 1982: Candidate of Sciences dissertation defended in Moscow
1984: published as 'The Other Side' (Al-Wajh al-Akhar)
Abbas later distanced himself from the figures and called the Holocaust an unforgivable crime (Haaretz, 2006)
Critics, including Netanyahu, still call him a Holocaust denier

title: Claim before the European Parliament that rabbis called for poisoning Palestinian water (2016)
description: In a speech to the European Parliament in Brussels on 23 June 2016, Abbas repeated a press report, which proved false, that rabbis in Israel had called for Palestinian wells to be poisoned (Haaretz). Netanyahu said he had spread a 'blood libel'. The next day Abbas's office retracted the statement, acknowledging that the claim was unfounded and saying he 'didn't intend to do harm to Judaism or to offend Jewish people around the world' (The New York Times).
key_facts: 23 June 2016: claim made in a speech at the European Parliament
Netanyahu: 'blood libel'
24 June 2016: retraction by Abbas's office

title: Palestinian National Council speech attributing persecution of Jews to their 'social function' (2018)
description: In a long speech opening a rare session of the Palestinian National Council in Ramallah on 30 April 2018, Abbas said that the Holocaust and the persecution of Jews in Europe were caused not by antisemitism but by Jews' 'social behaviour, [charging] interest and financial matters', and repeated the claim that Ashkenazi Jews descend from the Khazars, according to The Times of Israel, which reported the passage first; it did not appear in WAFA's English press release. Netanyahu, US Ambassador David Friedman, the EU, Germany and the United Nations criticised the speech, and The New York Times called for his resignation in an editorial. On 4 May 2018 his office issued an apology: 'If people were offended by my statement… especially people of the Jewish faith, I apologize to them', condemning antisemitism 'in all its forms' and calling the Holocaust 'the most heinous crime in history'.
key_facts: 30 April 2018: speech at the opening of the PNC's 23rd session
Condemned by Israel, the US ambassador, the EU, Germany and the UN
4 May 2018: apology 'if people were offended'

title: '50 holocausts' remark at the Berlin press conference with Olaf Scholz (2022)
description: Asked in Berlin on 16 August 2022 whether he would apologise for the 1972 Munich Olympics attack by the Black September group, then linked to Fatah, Abbas replied that Israel had committed '50 massacres, 50 slaughters, 50 holocausts' in Palestinian villages since 1947. Chancellor Olaf Scholz, who stood beside him without responding, later said he was 'disgusted' and condemned the remark as a trivialisation of the Holocaust; the Israeli foreign ministry also condemned it. Abbas then issued a statement calling the Holocaust 'the most heinous crime in modern history'. Berlin police opened a preliminary incitement investigation, which prosecutors closed in November 2022 (see justice).
key_facts: 16 August 2022: remark at the Chancellery in Berlin
Scholz: 'disgusted'; Israel condemns
Abbas statement: the Holocaust is 'the most heinous crime in modern history'
November 2022: Berlin prosecutors close the preliminary investigation

title: Fatah Revolutionary Council speech on Hitler's motives and the origins of Ashkenazi Jews (2023)
description: In a speech to Fatah's Revolutionary Council in Ramallah on 26 August 2023, aired on Palestinian television and translated by the Middle East Media Research Institute, Abbas said Hitler and Europe had fought the Jews 'because of their social role and not their religion', referring to 'usury, money and so on', and that Ashkenazi Jews 'are not Semites'. US antisemitism envoy Deborah Lipstadt called the remarks 'hateful, antisemitic'; the EU said they contained 'false and grossly misleading remarks about Jews' that 'trivialize' the Holocaust; France called them 'clearly unacceptable' and Germany's ambassador to Israel said Palestinians 'deserve to hear the historical truth from their leader'. On 7 September 2023 Paris Mayor Anne Hidalgo withdrew the city's Grand Vermeil medal awarded to him in 2015.
key_facts: 26 August 2023: speech to the Fatah Revolutionary Council
Condemned by the US, the EU, France, Germany and Israel
7 September 2023: Paris withdraws his Grand Vermeil medal

title: Dismissal of the Hamas-led unity government and rule by emergency decree after the 2007 split
description: After Hamas fighters seized control of the Gaza Strip from Fatah-led PA forces in June 2007, Abbas dismissed the national unity government of Prime Minister Ismail Haniyeh (formed in March 2007 under the Mecca Agreement), declared a state of emergency, outlawed Hamas's militia and appointed Salam Fayyad prime minister. Anis al-Qasem, a lawyer who drafted the Basic Law, and Hamas argued that the appointment was illegal because the Basic Law requires the Legislative Council's confidence, which Fayyad's government never received; Haniyeh continued to govern in Gaza. Western donors resumed aid to the West Bank government. Britannica notes that he has since ruled the West Bank by presidential decree and that in 2017, as a reconciliation deal faltered, he imposed his own sanctions on the Gaza Strip, adding to the Israeli and Egyptian restrictions. Hamas is designated a terrorist organisation by the United States, the United Kingdom and other states.
key_facts: June 2007: Hamas takes control of Gaza; Abbas dismisses the Haniyeh government and declares a state of emergency
Fayyad government never approved by the Legislative Council
Reconciliation agreements of 2007 (Mecca), 2014 and 2017 not fully implemented
2017: PA measures against Gaza (Britannica)

title: Expired mandate and two decades without national elections (2009–2026)
description: Elected in January 2005 for four years, Abbas remained in office when his term expired on 9 January 2009, arguing that presidential and legislative elections had to be held together; Hamas said his term had ended and that Legislative Council Speaker Aziz Duwaik should act as president. In December 2009 the PLO Central Council extended his term until elections could be held. Planned elections were postponed in 2010, 2011–2012, 2014, 2018, 2021 and 2026. On 10 October 2026 he cancelled the legislative vote set for 28 November 2026 and moved legislative and presidential elections to 11 September 2027, citing Israeli measures (see promises). France 'regrets' the decision and called for elections 'without delay'; Australia, Canada, France and the United Kingdom rejected the postponement in a joint statement according to Wikipedia; Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar called Abbas a 'corrupt dictator' whose reasons were a 'ridiculous lie'; Mustafa Barghouti of the Palestinian National Initiative said Palestinians had been denied elections for two decades. In an August 2026 PCPSR poll cited by The National, 79% of respondents wanted him to resign.
key_facts: 9 January 2009: end of the four-year term
16 December 2009: PLO Central Council extends his term indefinitely
No presidential election since 2005 and no legislative election since 2006
10 October 2026: elections postponed to 11 September 2027

title: Cancellation of the 2021 legislative and presidential elections
description: On 29 April 2021, weeks before the first legislative elections in 15 years, Abbas postponed the May and July 2021 votes indefinitely, saying Israel had not agreed to let Palestinians in East Jerusalem vote. Hamas, which had refused to attend the leadership meeting, called the decision 'a coup against the path of national partnership'; EU foreign-policy chief Josep Borrell called it 'deeply disappointing' while asking Israel to allow voting in East Jerusalem. Marwan Barghouti and Mohammed Dahlan, who led rival lists drawn from Fatah, said Abbas feared defeat; analysts quoted by Al Jazeera say he avoids elections because he fears that Fatah would lose to Hamas. Britannica notes that prominent Fatah figures had formed competing lists before the postponement.
key_facts: 15 January 2021: elections called
29 April 2021: indefinite postponement, citing East Jerusalem
Hamas: 'coup'; EU: 'deeply disappointing'
June 2021 PCPSR poll: 69% wanted elections soon even without East Jerusalem voting

title: Death of the critic Nizar Banat in the custody of PA security forces (2021) and the crackdown on protests
description: Nizar Banat, an activist and outspoken critic of corruption in the PA, died on 24 June 2021 about an hour after a joint Preventive Security and General Intelligence unit broke into the house in the Hebron area where he was staying, beat him with batons and took him away, according to Amnesty International. Protests in Ramallah against President Abbas were dispersed with what Amnesty called excessive force, with dozens of demonstrators arrested. Fourteen low-ranking Preventive Security officers were charged before the Ramallah military court, and the trial opened in September 2021. The family withdrew from the proceedings in May 2022, saying they had lost trust in them. In June 2022 the military prosecution released the defendants (temporarily, according to Amnesty), citing COVID-19, a step the Independent Commission for Human Rights said had no basis in Palestinian law. In December 2022 the family asked the International Criminal Court to investigate. Amnesty said no senior officer had been questioned and called for a civilian trial. No verdict was found as of October 2026. Abbas is not a party to the proceedings; the case concerns forces under the authority he heads.
key_facts: 24 June 2021: Nizar Banat dies after his arrest and beating by PA security forces (Amnesty)
September 2021: trial of 14 officers opens before the Ramallah military court
May 2022: family withdraws; June 2022: defendants released
No verdict found as of October 2026; Abbas is not a party

title: Payments to prisoners and families of 'martyrs' ('pay for slay') and the disputed 2025 reform
description: For years the PA paid monthly stipends to Palestinians held in Israeli prisons, scaled to the length of their sentence, and to families of Palestinians killed or wounded in the conflict, including attackers. Israel and the United States call the system 'pay for slay' and say it incentivises attacks; the Taylor Force Act, passed by the US Congress during Trump's first term, bars aid to the PA while sentence-based payments continue, and Israel has withheld PA tax revenues over it, then all transfers since 2025. Days after his February 2025 decree abolishing them, Abbas said: 'If we are left with only one penny, it will be given to the prisoners and the martyrs.' The PA says the system has been dismantled and replaced by needs-based welfare; an audit by Alvarez & Marsal released in summary in July 2026 supported that view while noting payments under the old system in November 2025, for which Abbas fired Finance Minister Omar Bitar. The US State Department and Israel say payments continue through other channels, which the PA denies; prisoners' families have protested against the loss of stipends, and a Ramallah court ruled against the reform in 2026, a ruling the PA called non-binding and appealed.
key_facts: Taylor Force Act: US aid conditioned on ending sentence-based payments
10 February 2025: decree abolishing the system
November 2025: finance minister fired over payments under the old mechanism
July 2026: PA-commissioned audit finds needs-based eligibility; State Department says it 'cannot serve as any proof'

title: Corruption allegations against the PA leadership and the business activities of Abbas's sons
description: Reuters reported in 2009 that companies run by Abbas's sons had won contracts, some funded by the United States, and in a July 2012 US House subcommittee hearing titled 'Chronic Kleptocracy', Elliott Abrams testified that corruption in the PA had discouraged donors. Yasser Abbas sued Foreign Policy and the author Jonathan Schanzer for libel over a 2012 article on the family's wealth; a US federal judge dismissed the suit in 2013 under the District of Columbia's anti-SLAPP law (Abbas himself was not a party). The 2016 Panama Papers showed a $1 million holding by one of his sons in an offshore company linked to the PA (Wikipedia, citing Haaretz). Yasser Abbas contested the allegations in court; no court has found Mahmoud Abbas guilty of corruption, and no proceedings against him personally were found. In October 2026 Israel's foreign minister called him a 'corrupt dictator', and The National reports that he and his administration are 'widely regarded as corrupt and ineffective'.
key_facts: 2009: Reuters reports on US-funded contracts won by firms run by his sons
July 2012: 'Chronic Kleptocracy' hearing in the US House of Representatives
2013: Yasser Abbas's libel suit against Foreign Policy dismissed under anti-SLAPP law
No proceedings against Abbas personally

title: Succession by decree: the vice-presidency for Hussein al-Sheikh and the election of his son Yasser to Fatah's leadership
description: In November 2024 Abbas named PNC Speaker Rawhi Fattouh as acting president in case of vacancy; in April 2025 he had the PLO create a vice-presidency and appointed his closest aide Hussein al-Sheikh, his point man with Israel, and in October 2025 a constitutional declaration made al-Sheikh interim president for up to 90 days in case of vacancy. The Guardian wrote that the closed-door decision was likely to reinforce the image of Fatah's ageing leadership as out of touch, and polls show al-Sheikh is deeply unpopular. At Fatah's eighth conference in May 2026, his son Yasser Abbas, a businessman based mainly in Canada who had been his 'special representative' but never held a Fatah post, was elected to the Central Committee, which Al Jazeera said raised questions about nepotism; The National reported concerns that he was being positioned for the succession. A Birzeit University political scientist told Al Jazeera that the seat alone did not put Yasser Abbas on a path to the presidency.
key_facts: 28 November 2024: Rawhi Fattouh named interim successor
26 April 2025: Hussein al-Sheikh appointed vice-president
26 October 2025: Constitutional Declaration No. 1 of 2025
May 2026: Yasser Abbas elected to Fatah's Central Committee

title: Concentration of power: dissolution of the Legislative Council and rule by decree
category: rule of law / separation of powers
description: With the Legislative Council idle since 2007, Abbas has legislated by decree-law. In December 2018 he announced that the Supreme Constitutional Court had dissolved the Council and called elections within six months, which were not held; Anis Kassim, editor of the Palestine Yearbook of International Law, called it 'a political decision not a legal one' and Hamas said it destroyed the political system. Britannica notes criticism of his rule as authoritarian, including crackdowns on organisers, journalists and social-media critics. In October 2026 Mustafa Barghouti told Al Jazeera that 'everything is concentrated in the hands of the executive authority', with 'no independent judiciary, no parliament'. The PA presents the draft interim constitution, with a two-term limit and separation of powers, as its answer.
key_facts: Legislative Council has not met since 2007
22 December 2018: dissolution of the Council announced
Decree-laws on elections, succession and welfare issued without a parliament
2026 draft interim constitution promises separation of powers

title: Security coordination with Israel and the PA's Jenin operation (2024–2025)
description: Security coordination with Israel, provided for under the Oslo framework, is widely unpopular among Palestinians; critics describe the PA as a subcontractor of Israel, while Israel and the United States regard coordination as a key element in containing attacks. Abbas has repeatedly announced its suspension (for example in January and July 2023), but The Times of Israel notes such suspensions were short-lived and that he told the CIA director in 2023 that parts remained in place. From early December 2024 PA security forces besieged the Jenin refugee camp in an operation against the 'Jenin Brigades', a coalition of armed groups including Hamas, Islamic Jihad and Fatah members, cutting water and electricity to most residents according to Al Jazeera; the PA said it aimed to restore 'law and order'. The PA then banned Al Jazeera's operations, and activists and rights groups reported dozens of people summoned or detained over social-media posts criticising the operation.
key_facts: January and July 2023: coordination suspended after Israeli raids in Jenin
December 2024: PA operation against armed groups in the Jenin camp
January 2025: PA bans Al Jazeera's operations
Rights groups report summonses and arrests over criticism

title: Clashes with US administrations: Jerusalem embassy, PLO office closure and visa denials
description: After welcoming Donald Trump in 2017, Abbas rejected US mediation when the Trump administration recognised Jerusalem as Israel's capital and announced the move of the US embassy in December 2017; in 2018 the United States cut aid to the PA and Palestinian programmes and closed the PLO office in Washington (Britannica). Relations improved under Joe Biden. In 2025, during Trump's second term, the State Department revoked the visas of Abbas and about 80 Palestinian officials before the UN General Assembly, citing national security; the Assembly voted 145–5 to let him speak by video, and the UN said the decision was contrary to the Headquarters Agreement. Abbas attended Trump's Gaza summit at Sharm el-Sheikh on 13 October 2025. In September 2026 he was again denied a visa and addressed the Assembly by recorded video, calling the US measures 'unlawful' and 'punitive'; the State Department said it was extending visa sanctions over the PA's actions at the ICC and the International Court of Justice, its pursuit of unilateral recognition and its payments and statements relating to terrorism.
key_facts: December 2017: PA rejects US mediation after the Jerusalem decision
September 2018: US closes the PLO office in Washington
September 2025: US revokes his visa; UN General Assembly allows a video address (145–5)
September 2026: visa denied again; speech by video
